## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.

- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.instead: Rows: 'Missed booking calls turned into bookings' · 'Calls answered after hours, at peak and on holidays'; Keel will test: For most, with it, their last reservation shift when a booking call went unanswered would have given them missed booking calls turned into bookings and calls answered after hours, at peak and on holidays.

screens.why1: After compatibility and relative advantage, asking what effort the agents take on to start is the obvious next solution question, and it was not asked before.
screens.why2: 'What will they have to do to start using it?' with 'setup, extra steps or learning' reads at once, and I could type my two steps straight off.
screens.why3: I know exactly what a desk or central office has to do to switch Codyco on: forward the missed calls and decide which calls come back to the desk.
screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip, 'Leave this out of the study', which does what the card's 'I'm not sure' does and fits a box I type into.
screens.why5: The screen frames my own words and asks nothing that bends them; what I typed is what will be carried forward.
screens.why7: The box keeps the card's count and length (up to four, 9 words each), but its hint invites 'any setup' without saying the step must be one the agents take themselves, which lets in a setup my team or the product does, as my second row half is, and that is the card's named pitfall.
screens.instead: What will reservation agents have to do themselves to start using it, such as a setup step, a new habit or something to learn? Up to four, each up to 9 words, not what your team or their director does. Chip: I'm not sure, leave this out.

screens.why1: Right after I said what they'd have to do to start, it's obvious Keel shows back the efforts it drafted from my answer so I can pick one to test.
screens.why2: Both rows are in a reservation agent's own words (missed booking calls, hands to the desk); 'the desk' reads a touch front-office for a central reservations office, but nobody would stumble on it.
screens.why3: Letting the AI take their missed booking calls is the agent's own daily habit, but deciding which calls the AI passes back is often set by the reservations lead or by us at onboarding, so an agent might partly guess.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, each one step, under 9 words, in 'their' voice, and nothing obvious missing at the 1-to-4 count.
screens.why5: The first row is the revision-24 wording I agreed to, and the second stays on my mechanism (the AI answers, hands back what it can't book) without leaking roles or product names a stranger wouldn't know.
screens.why7: Both rows sit on the one measure and pass the shape rules, but 'Set which calls the AI hands to the desk' leans toward a setup our team or the lead does rather than a step the agent takes themselves, and the new habit of use (checking what the AI booked) isn't offered.
screens.instead: Rows: 'Hand their missed booking calls to the AI' · 'Check the AI's bookings in the PMS each shift' -- the second asked as: you'd check the bookings it made in your PMS each shift.

screens.why1: After writing the efforts on the screens before, picking the one most likely to stop my reservation agents is the obvious next step before Keel tests it.
screens.why2: 'Missed booking calls', 'the AI' and 'the desk' are the words my agents and I use every shift, and both rows read on the first pass.
screens.why3: I know which of these my agents balk at: handing their guests to an AI is the one I hear pushback on, not the routing setting.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, both mine, in my words, neither overlapping, and the one I'd pick is there.
screens.why5: The first row and the belief say exactly what I meant, handing missed booking calls to the AI, and the belief is my pick unchanged.
screens.why7: Both rows are base-form, use 'their', and the belief fits the bar, but 'Set which calls the AI hands to the desk' reads like a routing setup my team or the group's admin does with the director rather than a step the agent takes, and handing missed calls to the AI sits close to Compatibility's call-forwarding row, so the shape bends without breaking.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? -- Hand their missed booking calls to the AI · Check the AI's bookings in the PMS each shift

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out is the obvious place to decide whether to collect people for a pilot, and my whole launch runs on a pilot at one location, so I expect to be asked.
screens.why2: Offer a pilot, yes or no, with the exact line respondents will see: plain on first read.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot leads is my own call, and I know I do.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers the choice, and the two options are distinct and clear.
screens.why5: My pilot is a paid €3,000 money-back pilot at one hotel, which the director decides and the owner agrees to, but the line is a generic 'try this for real, leave your email' put to reservation agents who don't pay, so my offer drifted a little.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes get: 'Would your hotel try this for real, as a money-back pilot at one hotel? Leave your email, or your reservations director's.' (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs in the last step before the study goes out, after the pilot offer and before people see it.
screens.why2: Pick a voice, hear a 5-second sample, 400 credits either way, link by text: I can read all of it at once.
screens.why3: It is my own study and my own credits, so I can hear both and choose.
screens.why4: The two voices are distinct and each has a sample, but nothing says which language or accent they speak, and my respondents are German reservation agents in Munich who would expect to be asked in German.
screens.why5: It still names reservation agents as the people asked, and nothing of Codyco or the AI receptionist leaks into the choice.
screens.instead: Who should ask reservation agents your questions, in German? Daphne (German, ▶ 5 s) · Saskia (German, ▶ 5 s)

screens.why1: Once I've picked who asks the questions, how my reservation agents will answer comes next, just before sending, so it's clear why it's here.
screens.why2: Each option says in a line what the agent will actually do (talk to Daphne on video, read and tap, or pick when they open the link), so I can choose on first reading even though the name Daphne means nothing to me until I read its line.
screens.why3: I know my agents take this on a phone or a front-desk PC between calls, so I can judge whether a tap-through suits them better than talking on video at the desk.
screens.why4: Video with Daphne, text, or letting them choose covers the real choices, the three don't overlap, and my pick, Read and tap, is there as written.
screens.why5: It's a setting about the study's format; nothing of my product, its AI phone agent or the director who pays leaks into what the agents will see.

screens.why1: Last screen of the send flow, after choosing who asks and how they answer, so asking who gets a link is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Plain words; 'Contacts page' is Keel's own page, named the same way the earlier screens name it.
screens.why3: I know whether I have reservation agents at hotel groups I can name or would rather post in a hospitality group, so I can answer from my own situation.
screens.why4: The three ways to reach people (by name, a Keel list, one open link) are distinct, complete for sending, and none needs an escape chip.
screens.why5: Nothing of Codyco's product or roles leaks, and my pick, people I know by name, is kept as I picked it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits beside a tally of 3 of 3 holding, but the number that decides it is Relative advantage at exactly 5 of 7, the bar, and that number is down in card 2, not next to the verdict.
screens.why_b2: Each card plainly says what was counted (said yes / would have gone better / would do it), over 7 people, and where the bar sits (5 of 7), so I read all three at first look.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names are mine, but my statement reads broken ('the reservation agent the AI reservation agent answers… and gets back the confirmed booking'), and the Relative advantage line ('their last guest call would have given them missed calls turned into bookings') is mangled, though I can still recognise it.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do now: not to go to the director with the €3,000 pilot, and not to probe the 3 agents whose handover came with a condition or the 2 who saw no gain.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible and 'at the bar' is honest, but the headline 'Holding up' over 3 of 3 reads as a clean pass. The weakest belief only just clears at 5 of 7, and nothing says that 7 agents is a small read.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: Relative advantage clears at exactly 5 of 7 and 3 of the 6 who would hand over calls want a condition, so ask those 3 what the condition is before you pitch the €3,000 pilot to the director.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said yes, easily or most of the time · bar 5 of 7', so I see both the result and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 people, and the strip marks my bar at 5 of 7 with 6 cells for and 1 against, so all three read on first look.
screens.why_b3: The title is Compatibility and the belief, 'Most reservation agents could forward unanswered calls to another number', is the condition I checked, though the bar line 'You said could forward…' drops its subject.
screens.why_b4: The So line points me to Adoption friction, which is useful, but it reads garbled ('Whether could forward…') and says nothing about Aylin's case of an old phone system the owner won't pay to replace, which is a concrete roll-out problem I'd need to plan for.
screens.why_b5: The count line keeps n visible and says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', but the So line then states flatly that forwarding 'is not what will stop them' on 7 answers, with one person already saying it would stop her.
screens.instead: Holding up, a lean: 6 of 7 could forward missed calls (bar 5 of 7); one desk's old phone system can't without IT and a new system, so plan forwarding setup for hotels like hers. The bigger open question is Adoption friction, below.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 5 of 7 for, the bar of 5 of 7 and 'at the bar', so I know it held, but only just, and why.
screens.why_b2: Better 5 (all a lot), Same 1 and Worse 1 over 7, with the strip's marker at 5, read at a glance, though 'Same' is not the 'No difference' the rule line uses.
screens.why_b3: Both my benefits are there, but the occasion is 'their last guest call' rather than the last unanswered booking call the question actually asked about, and 'a call would have given them missed calls turned into bookings' reads oddly.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates 5 of 7 and points me to Adoption friction, but it does not say I am exactly at the bar or that the two against are a group already covered by a call center and an agent who won't hand guests to a machine.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 stays visible, it says 'a lean, not a call' and that it is a hypothetical, and a pass exactly at the bar is not called strong.
screens.instead: Belief: 'their last unanswered booking call'; So: 'Held exactly at the bar, 5 of 7, all a lot better. The two against are a group whose call center already covers after six and an agent who won't hand guests to a machine, so test groups without after-hours cover and see Adoption friction below.'

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 and bar 5 of 7, and with only Tobias against I am well inside the no-more-than-1-in-3 rule, so the verdict and its number agree.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 people, all 7 counted, and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against, with the marker at 5, all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would hand their missed booking calls to the AI' are the belief I picked, word for word, and the question asks it of the agents in the same terms.
screens.why_b4: The So line promises that what would make it worth it to those 3 is below, but below is only the same condition repeated three times, so I am not told the concrete move: hand calls that need an agent's judgement back to the desk, and find out what put Tobias off.
screens.why_b5: The low n is said ('a lean, not a call') and the conditional yeses are split out, but 'Only if missed calls need your own judgement' reads backwards for an agent (it sounds like they would hand calls over only when the calls need their judgement), so half the 'for' may hide a real catch that the screen counts as a plain yes.
screens.instead: Holding up, 6 of 7, but 3 only if the calls that need their own judgement come back to them, so build a clean handback for those (and ask Tobias why not) before calling this settled with 7 people.

screens.why_b1: Each box gives its verdict, Holding up, with the deciding count right beside it (6 of 7 against a bar of 5, and 5 of 7 at the bar), and the lead-in sentence ties the number to the verdict again.
screens.why_b3: The Compatibility belief is the call-forwarding line I checked, but the Relative advantage line reads as a mangled template ('their last guest call would have given them missed calls turned into bookings'); I recognise it, but it isn't how I'd say it.
screens.why_b4: The screen lists the dissenters and stops; it never says what an un-forwardable phone system or a guest who wants a person means for the pilot, so I'm left to work out the next step myself.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 stays visible, but the lead-in 'Relative advantage held, 5 of 7' drops the 'at the bar' the status line carries, and nowhere does it say that 7 people is a thin base for calling either belief held.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add things I did not type: forwarding needs IT and an owner who won't pay for a new phone system; some guests ring precisely for a person who knows the house; and where a call center already covers after six, the real pain is group requests and emails without rates.

screens.why1: As the first screen it checks whether I work where the study is aimed, which is the obvious thing to ask before anything else.
screens.why2: Hotel group, central reservations office and call center are everyday words in my job at a Munich central reservations office, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I know for certain whether my employer is a German hotel group that runs a central reservations office, because I sit in it.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it completely for a gate question, and the gate correctly has no escape.
screens.why5: It repeats the founder's segment in plain trade words and reveals nothing about any product or plan.
screens.why6: It is one short question of 18 words with two options anyone can hold, though the guidelines' screener form would end on a simpler 'Yes or no.' instead of 'I'll read 2 options.'

screens.why1: A screen about a recent week fits right after the office question, but asking whether a booking call came in is pointless for someone who takes them all shift long, and the next screen suddenly asks about a call nobody answered.
screens.why2: Plain words from my desk: booking call, shift, last 7 days.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether calls came in on my shifts this week; they came in all Saturday at the trade fair.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it and do not overlap; the two chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this gate.
screens.why5: The founder counted calls that went unanswered, but this asks only whether a call came in at all, so the problem itself has dropped out of the question.
screens.why6: Short, one question, said once and answered with yes or no.
screens.why7: The gate asks the circumstance every agent is in, so everyone says Yes and No has no one; the founder's belief can never be refuted, exactly the card's bad example.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call come in on your shift that nobody answered? Yes · No

screens.why1: After two screens about booking calls on my shift, it makes sense to show me the idea about the calls nobody answers before asking me what I think of it.
screens.why2: PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot and Apaleo are words I use every day at the reservations desk, and the rest is plain German-office talk once translated; only 'by your hotel's rules' is a little vague about which rules are meant.
screens.why3: I take booking calls on every shift and I know a Saturday at fair time when the line rings and nobody can get to it, so I can judge this from my own work.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It is clearly shown as the idea on purpose, and the belief repeats the circumstance of calls not getting answered; nothing of the founder's plan reaches me outside the card.
screens.why6: Heard once, seven sentences is long, and the line listing three PMS names is a mouthful that adds little when spoken; 'hands a call to your desk by your hotel's rules' is awkward to catch by ear.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, an AI reservation agent that answers the calls nobody picks up. When nobody picks up, the call goes to it; it answers the guest in your hotel's voice, takes the payment and books straight into your PMS, and passes a call to your desk when your rules say so. The people building it believe it would answer the calls nobody at your hotel picks up.

screens.why1: Asking whether missed calls can be sent elsewhere makes sense right after an AI that picks up the calls nobody answers, but tying it to my last guest call is abrupt, because that call I picked up myself.
screens.why2: Forwarding calls to another number is plain office talk to me, but 'could you have' on one call I answered makes me read it twice to work out what is meant.
screens.why3: In our central office the routing and overflow on the phone system are set by IT or the team lead, not by me, so I would partly be guessing what the setup allows.
screens.why4: My true answer is 'only if IT or my lead sets it up', and 'Only sometimes' does not say that; I would end up picking No or I can't tell.
screens.why5: 'The calls nobody picks up' says plainly what the founder meant by calls that do not get answered, and nothing else of the product leaks.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, and four short options plus the escape that I can hold after hearing them once.
screens.why7: Forwarding is something the phone setup allows or needs sign-off for, so it is a permission, yet it is served the ability scale without 'Only with help or approval', though the four codes, their order and the separate I can't tell are right.
screens.instead: Think of your last busy shift. Could unanswered calls have been sent on to another number? Yes, easily · Yes, with some steps · Only with help or approval · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the idea card it asks whether this AI would have helped with the very thing it is for, a call nobody picked up, so it is obvious why it comes here.
screens.why2: "Done that better" made me stop, because nobody did anything with an unanswered call, so I had to read it again to see it means "handled that call better".
screens.why3: On a trade-fair Saturday I see the abandoned calls stacking up on the queue display, so I know well what an unanswered booking call is and can judge whether something picking it up would have helped.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover every answer I could give without overlap, and "I can't tell" fits if I don't trust it.
screens.why5: It names Codyco as the card did and asks nothing in anyone else's words, so nothing of the plan leaks beyond the idea I was shown on purpose.
screens.why6: Two short sentences and four short options read as a list, then the one escape, which I can hear once and answer.
screens.why7: The occasion is the missed call the advantage is for, the four fixed answers come in order with No difference and Worse so the belief can be held or refuted, and I can't tell is the one escape.
screens.instead: Think of the last booking call on your shift that nobody picked up. Would Codyco, an AI reservation agent, have handled that call better for you, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After the idea card and the question about whether it would have done better, asking whether I'd actually let it take my missed calls is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: 'Hand your missed booking calls to it' needs a second read, because a missed call is one nobody took, so I can't hand it to anyone; in our office we'd say the calls nobody picks up go to it.
screens.why3: Partly: I know which calls slip through on a trade-fair Saturday, but where unanswered calls go is set by our supervisor and the phone system, not by me at the desk, so I'd be half guessing.
screens.why4: 'Only if missed calls need your own judgement' is backwards: if a call needs my judgement, that is exactly when I wouldn't hand it to a machine, so as a yes it makes no sense.
screens.why5: It still means the founder's idea of an AI taking the calls nobody picks up, and nothing of their plan or their own terms for us leaks through.
screens.why6: Short and one question, but 'only if missed calls need your own judgement' is a mouthful that I'd have to replay in my head to see which way it cuts.
screens.why7: Four options in order with the one escape, and the belief can go either way, but the Only-if condition is inverted so it doesn't work as a conditional yes, and routing the calls is half my supervisor's step rather than an effort I take myself.
screens.instead: To use Codyco, you'd let it take the booking calls nobody picks up. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Only if it passed tricky guests back to me · Probably not · No · I can't tell
